Ohio Economy Dashboard

Conditions and a one-year statistical outlook for Ohio, its large metros, and the U.S.

Data through Sep 2026 · Updated Sep 27, 2026

At a glance

Snapshot for Aug 2026: a mid-cycle expansion with a still-tight labor market. Currently: labor still tight; activity on the firm side; inflation near normal; ordinary house-price growth. That reading is backed by low unemployment, low UI claims, firm activity growth. Over the next year the central paths lean toward a bit more cooling in activity, with labor still relatively steady. No clear recession-style warning in the major labor and activity paths. Further regional detail is available from the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, including its SORCE survey and the Fourth District Beige Book.

Scorecard

One-glance read aligned with the summary above. Green = favorable, yellow = caution, red = concerning.

Ohio Industry Composition (GDP shares)

As of 2025, Ohio’s largest GDP contributors include Finance, insurance & real estate, Manufacturing, Professional & business services. Manufacturing alone is about 14% of Ohio GDP versus roughly 9% nationally—Ohio remains a goods-heavy state. Finance/real estate and health care are large service anchors alongside professional services and government. Shares are current-dollar BEA GDP by industry (structural snapshot, not a monthly cycle gauge).

Annual GDP by industry, current dollars (BEA Regional table SAGDP2N). Bars show each sector’s share of statewide (or U.S.) GDP for the latest available year (2025). Top sectors by Ohio share; U.S. shares shown for comparison. Source: BEA GDP by State.

Ohio Goods Trade Trends

In 2025, Ohio shipped about $57 billion in goods exports. Exports were about -2% versus 2024. Goods imports were about $87 billion the same year (merchandise trade deficit of roughly $31 billion). Manufactured goods account for the bulk of shipments (about 94% of exports). On the latest detailed partner snapshot (2022), the largest markets include Canada (34%), Mexico (13%), Japan (6%), China (5%). Trade data are merchandise only (not services), concentrated in vehicles, machinery, and other industrial products.

Annual totals of monthly Census goods trade for Ohio (FRED EXPTOTOH / IMPTOTOH), calendar years with full 12 months. Partner shares use Census/Origin-of-Movement annual series via FRED (latest detailed year). Source: FRED / U.S. Census Bureau.

Fourth District Business Survey (Cleveland Fed SORCE)

As of the Aug 2026 survey wave, Cleveland Fed SORCE diffusion indexes summarize whether more Fourth District contacts report increases than decreases in current conditions, employment, and expected conditions (positive = net expansion among respondents). These timely survey readings complement the hard data above. Coverage is the Federal Reserve’s Fourth District (all of Ohio plus parts of PA, KY, and WV).

Seasonally adjusted diffusion indexes from the Cleveland Fed Survey of Regional Conditions and Expectations (SORCE) for the Total sector. Index = percent reporting increases minus percent reporting decreases (range −100 to +100; zero ≈ balance). Released about eight times per year. Source: Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland — SORCE (doi:10.26509/frbc-sorce). The six seasonally adjusted Total-sector indexes also enter the model as survey series.

Experimental downturn signal (not a calibrated probability) — click to expand

Experimental Ohio downturn signal (not a calibrated probability)

As of Sep 2026, the signal for a current coincident-index decline reads 0%. This is a model score, not a calibrated probability: in pseudo-real-time evaluation it ranked downturn months much worse than in-sample and was no better than the historical base rate (12% of months since 2000). The coincident index is published through Aug 2026.

A probit model of an Ohio downturn month, defined as a fall in the Philadelphia Fed Ohio coincident index over the previous three months (shaded), on the 3-month average of the model's national and Ohio factors (national1, national2, ohio1, ohio2), for the current month only. COVID months are excluded from estimation and blanked in the chart. In-sample fit uses smoothed factors and greatly overstates real-time accuracy (see Methods §5b); this is an experimental signal, not a calibrated probability.

Methodology & model details

This dashboard reports forecasts from a hierarchical mixed-frequency dynamic factor model (MF-DFM) estimated on Ohio, Midwest, and national series from FRED and other public sources. The state unit is monthly. Quarterly series are observed only in quarter-end months (March, June, September, December); other months are missing for those series. Charts show rate levels or year-over-year percent growth only (never QoQ/MoM).

Cleveland MSA geography: Cleveland series follow the current OMB delineation (Bulletin 23-01), Cleveland, OH (CBSA 17410; BLS area 391741). Series for the former Cleveland-Elyria definition are not used, except Indeed job postings, which Indeed publishes only under the former code 17460.

1. Observation equation (estimation space)

Let \(i\) index series and \(t\) months. After transform and standardization, the observation equation is

\[ z_{i,t} = \alpha_i + \Lambda_i' F_t + \varepsilon_{i,t} \]

where \(z_{i,t}\) is the demeaned/scaled estimation-space series, \(F_t\) is the vector of latent factors active for series \(i\) (see loading table), \(\Lambda_i\) are free loadings on those factors (zeros elsewhere), and \(\varepsilon_{i,t}\) is idiosyncratic noise. Fourier seasonal terms (annual and semi-annual harmonics) are residualized from the panel before factor extraction so latent factors are non-seasonal; the same terms re-enter the observation regression and series forecasts. Optional COVID dummies may also enter in sample; forecasts set COVID dummies to zero.

Transforms into estimation space:

  • Growth / index series: \(g_t = 100\,\log(Y_t / Y_{t-1})\) (monthly) or QoQ log growth at quarter ends.
  • Rate series (unemployment, yields, fed funds): \(\Delta r_t = r_t - r_{t-1}\) (first difference; avoids mean-reversion of levels to the long historical average).

Each transformed series is standardized using means and standard deviations computed from 2000-01-01 onward (hard COVID window excluded from location/scale).

2. Factor hierarchy and extraction

Factors are extracted stagewise by residualized EM-PCA, then loadings are estimated by OLS with the hierarchy mask:

  1. National factors \(F_t^{\mathrm{N}}\) from the national panel only. Residualize all series on \(F^{\mathrm{N}}\).
  2. Ohio residual factors \(F_t^{\mathrm{OH}}\) from non-national residuals. Residualize non-national series on \(F^{\mathrm{OH}}\).
  3. MSA residual factors \(F_t^{m}\) for each metro \(m\) in {cleveland, columbus, cincinnati, other Ohio metros (pooled)} from that metro’s residual panel. Residualize those series on \(F^{m}\). Akron, Dayton, Toledo, Youngstown and Canton share a single pooled factor (othermetros1); their series are too few and too noisy for one factor each.
  4. Sector block factors \(F_t^{b}\) for \(b\) in {labor, prices, housing, activity, consumption} from residualized series in each block.
  • National factors: 2
  • Ohio residual factors: 2
  • MSA residual factors: 1 each for cleveland, columbus, cincinnati, other Ohio metros (pooled)
  • Block factors: 1 per block (labor, prices, housing, activity, consumption)
  • Total factors: 13 — national1, national2, ohio1, ohio2, cleveland1, columbus1, cincinnati1, othermetros1, labor1, prices1, housing1, activity1, consumption1

Estimated factor paths (history and short-horizon forecasts) for each layer of the hierarchy are plotted on a companion page: factor paths.

3. Which series load on which factors

✓ = free loading estimated; blank / — = restricted to zero. “Own block” is the series’ sector block (labor, prices, housing, activity or consumption).

Series groupNational
national*		Ohio residual
ohio*		MSA residualSector block
labor* etc.
National (US GDP, CPI, UNRATE, FEDFUNDS, …)✓———
Ohio state / regional (OHUR, OHRQGSP, Midwest CPI, …)✓✓—own block
Cleveland MSA series✓✓own only
cleveland*		own block
Columbus MSA series✓✓own only
columbus*		own block
Cincinnati MSA series✓✓own only
cincinnati*		own block
Other Ohio metros (pooled) series✓✓own only
othermetros*		own block

Compactly, for a series with allowed factor set \(S_i\):

\[ z_{i,t} = \alpha_i + \sum_{k \in S_i} \lambda_{i,k} f_{k,t} + \varepsilon_{i,t} \]

\(S_i\) = national factors only for national series; national + Ohio residual + own block for state/regional series; national + Ohio + own MSA residual + own block for MSA series.

4. Factor dynamics (sparse VARX)

Factors follow a sparse hierarchical VARX (not independent ARs):

\[ F_t = c + \sum_{j=1}^{p} \Phi_j F_{t-j} + \Gamma X_{t-1} + u_t \]
  • Lag order: \(p = 1\) (selected by sparse-VARX BIC over candidates [1, 2, 3, 4]; common sample, hierarchical lag restrictions; picks by criterion on this run: BIC p=1, AIC p=4, HQIC p=3; candidates with a companion root of 1 or more are rejected; re-selected at every estimation)
  • Sparsity: national factors depend only on national lags; Ohio on national+Ohio; each MSA on national+Ohio+own MSA; blocks on national+Ohio+own block.
  • Exogenous \(X\) (national financial and activity indicators, lag 1, in Ohio/MSA/block equations): FEDFUNDS, GS10, INDPRO, PAYEMS, UNRATE (AR(1) for multi-step \(X\) paths). Broader national cycle indicators (CFNAI, leading and financial-conditions indexes, the term spread, the Sahm rule, the NY Fed WEI) are not model inputs: in pseudo-real-time evaluation they did not improve short-horizon accuracy and reduced 12-month accuracy.
  • Stability: if the fitted VARX has a companion root at or above 1, its lag matrices are shrunk until the system is stationary.
  • Kalman smoother: factors refined by a joint linear Gaussian filter/smoother given hierarchical loadings and the VARX law (Mariano–Murasawa poly for quarterly series).
  • Extraction weights: majors up-weighted in EM-PCA (×3).

5. Idiosyncratic residual, direct multi-horizon, and forecasts

Let \(\hat\varepsilon_{i,T}\) be the last in-sample residual in estimation space. Forecasts add a decaying AR(1) residual path so short-horizon forecasts do not jump from the last data point to the pure common component:

\[ \hat\varepsilon_{i,T+h} = \rho_i^{h} \hat\varepsilon_{i,T}, \qquad \hat z_{i,T+h} = \alpha_i + \Lambda_i' \hat F_{T+h} + \hat\varepsilon_{i,T+h} \]

Direct multi-horizon: for major indicators, also estimate \(z_{i,T+h} = a_{i,h} + b_{i,h}' F_T\) by OLS for \(h \in \{1,2,3,4,5,6,9,12\}\) and blend with the iterated VARX common-component path.

Unpublished months: series are released with different lags, so the panel ends at \(T\) while many series stop earlier. For each series, the months after its last release through \(T\) are filled with the model nowcast (smoothed common component, seasonal term and decaying residual); forecasts for \(T+1, T+2, \dots\) continue from there. On the charts, the forecast line therefore starts at the first unpublished month.

Factors are iterated with the sparse VARX (Monte Carlo draws of shocks for bands). Mapping back to levels (\(Y_T\) is the last published value):

  • Growth series: compound from last level, \(Y_{T+h} = Y_T \cdot \exp\!\big(\sum \hat g / 100\big)\); quarterly growth is applied as \(g/3\) per month for a monthly latent path (MM used in Kalman measurement).
  • Rate series: \(r_{T+h} = r_T + \sum \widehat{\Delta r}\).

Dashboard display for indexes is year-over-year growth of the level path, \(100\,\log(Y_t / Y_{t-12})\). Confidence bands: 350 Monte Carlo simulations; 68% (16th–84th) and faint outer 95% (2.5th–97.5th) percentiles. Chart history ≈ 3 years, January-aligned; forecast horizon 12 months.

5b. Experimental turning-point (downturn) signal

An Ohio downturn month is defined as \(D_t = 1\) when the Philadelphia Fed Ohio coincident index (OHPHCI) is below its level three months earlier. A probit \(\Pr(D_t=1 \mid F_t) = \Phi(a + b' \bar F_t)\) is estimated, where \(\bar F_t\) is the 3-month average of the national and Ohio factors (national1, national2, ohio1, ohio2). Because the factors are Kalman-smoothed to the edge of the panel, the signal extends to months the coincident index has not yet reached. COVID months (March 2020 to June 2021) are excluded; an L1-regularized probit is used if separation occurs. Real-time caveat: in a pseudo-real-time (vintage) backtest, 2000–2026, the nowcast's ability to rank downturn months fell from an in-sample AUC of about 0.95 to about 0.74, and its Brier score was no better than always predicting the historical base rate. The output is therefore shown only as an experimental current-month signal, not a calibrated probability, and is not used in the headline summary.

Latest estimate (factors through Sep 2026; coincident index through Aug 2026): 0%. In-sample McFadden pseudo-R²: 0.85. Share of downturn months since 2000: 12%.

6. Sample & robustness

  • Weekly data: Ohio initial claims, continued claims and the insured unemployment rate (OHINSUREDUR) enter as the monthly mean of complete weeks; the current month is missing until its last week is published.
  • Data vintage: every estimation uses the latest published values, including revisions.
  • Estimation sample: 2000-01-31 to 2026-09-30 (193 series after filters)
  • Factor sample start: 2000-01-01
  • COVID handling: dummies (2020-03-01–2020-12-31; soft tail to 2021-06-30)
  • Growth / Δr winsorization: 0.5% tails; standardized inputs are then clipped at ±5 standard deviations
  • Metro charts: Cleveland, Columbus and Cincinnati show unemployment, payrolls, manufacturing payrolls, a house price index and Zillow rents and home values (Cleveland also the labor force); Akron, Dayton, Toledo, Youngstown and Canton show unemployment and payrolls.

7. Data sources

Series used in estimation and on this page (free public APIs and open data files):

  • FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis) — fred.stlouisfed.org · API docs: docs (Ohio/MSA/national labor, housing, GDP, CPI, rates, weekly UI claims and insured unemployment rate, etc.)
  • BLS Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS) — bls.gov/jlt · Public API: developers (U.S. job openings rate; state JOLTS are released only annually and are not used)
  • EIA electricity retail sales — eia.gov/opendata (Ohio total and industrial sales, MWh)
  • BEA Regional Economic Accounts — bea.gov regional · API: API signup (Ohio real GDP and personal income; metro regional price parities)
  • Zillow Research public data — zillow.com/research/data (ZORI rents and ZHVI home values for Cleveland, Columbus, Cincinnati metros; attribution to Zillow Research required)
  • Census / BLS via FRED — high-propensity business applications and other formation series where available (e.g. BAHBATOTALSAOH on FRED)
  • BEA GDP by State (industry) — bea.gov (annual current-dollar GDP by industry for Ohio industry-composition panel)
  • U.S. Census goods trade (via FRED) — EXPTOTOH / IMPTOTOH monthly goods exports and imports for Ohio (annualized on the trade-trends panel; partner shares from Census SCEN series)
  • Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland — SORCE (Survey of Regional Conditions and Expectations) — SORCE page · doi:10.26509/frbc-sorce (Fourth District diffusion indexes; all of Ohio plus parts of PA, KY, WV; plotted on this dashboard; the six seasonally adjusted Total-sector indexes also enter the model)

7b. Additional regional series

Further open-data series enter the model: payrolls, unemployment and housing indicators for Akron, Dayton, Toledo, Youngstown and Canton; Cleveland house prices, permits and listings; Indeed job postings (the labor-demand indicator; monthly means of complete weeks); Cleveland Fed SORCE indexes; Ohio goods exports; quarterly QCEW wages, BEA wages and salaries and Census tax collections (Mariano–Murasawa); and an Ohio consumption/fiscal block with the S-1 county sales-tax base (validated against published county totals; metro aggregates load on their metro factor), Census state retail sales and Ohio OBM monthly tax receipts. OBM employer withholding changes basis in July 2023; that month's growth rate is treated as a level shift (missing), and the source gap in August 2018 is left to the Kalman filter. Series that are not seasonally adjusted are adjusted within each estimation by removing calendar-month (quarterly: calendar-quarter) means of their growth rates, estimated on that estimation's sample, in addition to the model's Fourier terms.

  • BLS CES via FRED: 5 series (monthly; block labor; other Ohio metros); typical release lag ~4-5 weeks.
  • BLS LAUS via FRED: 5 series (monthly; block labor; other Ohio metros); typical release lag ~5-6 weeks.
  • FHFA HPI master file: 8 series (monthly, quarterly; block housing; Cleveland, Ohio, other Ohio metros, regional); typical release lag ~2 months; ~2 months after quarter.
  • Zillow Research: 4 series (monthly; block housing; other Ohio metros); typical release lag mid-following month.
  • Census BPS metro files: 2 series (monthly; block housing; Cleveland, other Ohio metros); typical release lag ~3 weeks.
  • Realtor.com Residential Data: 3 series (monthly; block housing; Cleveland); typical release lag first week of following month.
  • Indeed Hiring Lab: 9 series (monthly; block labor; Cincinnati, Cleveland, Columbus, Ohio, other Ohio metros); typical release lag ~1 week.
  • Cleveland Fed SORCE: 6 series (monthly; block activity, labor, prices; regional); typical release lag ~1 week after each survey wave (~8 waves/yr).
  • Census state exports via FRED: 1 series (monthly; block activity; Ohio); typical release lag ~5 weeks.
  • BLS QCEW open data: 1 series (quarterly; block activity; Ohio); typical release lag ~5-6 months after quarter.
  • BEA via FRED: 1 series (quarterly; block activity; Ohio); typical release lag ~3 months after quarter.
  • Census QTAX via FRED: 1 series (quarterly; block activity; Ohio); typical release lag ~3 months after quarter.
  • Ohio Dept. of Taxation S-1 (county permissive sales tax): 5 series (monthly; block consumption; Cincinnati, Cleveland, Columbus, Ohio, other Ohio metros); typical release lag ~2.5-3 months (collections in m mostly reflect sales in m-1).
  • Census Monthly State Retail Sales (experimental): 1 series (monthly; block consumption; Ohio); typical release lag ~2.5-3 months.
  • Ohio OBM Monthly Financial Report (GRF receipts): 3 series (monthly; block consumption; Ohio); typical release lag ~10 days.

Cleveland charts use the current Cleveland, OH metro definition (BLS area 17410). Geography details are in the Cleveland note above.
